# @tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime

A Temporal-backed execution engine for Node-RED flows. It boots a real,
unmodified Node-RED runtime headlessly, and uses the `preRoute`/`onComplete`
hook seam (`RED.hooks`) to let a Temporal Workflow drive message delivery
one node at a time, instead of Node-RED's own local routing.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js >= 22.9 (see `engines` in `package.json`).
- A running Temporal server, reachable at `127.0.0.1:7233` by default
  (override with the `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS` env var). Either:
  - the [Temporal CLI](https://docs.temporal.io/cli)'s dev server:
    `temporal server start-dev`, or
  - a real Temporal cluster.
- Dependencies installed at the repo root: `npm install` (this package is
  not a separate npm workspace; it is hoisted into the repo's flat
  `packages/node_modules/` layout and depends on the sibling `@node-red/*`
  packages via normal `require()`).

## Command sequence

All commands below are run from this package's directory,
`packages/node_modules/@tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime/`.

1. Start (or reuse) a Temporal dev server in one terminal:

   ```bash
   temporal server start-dev
   ```

   This also serves the Temporal Web UI at `http://localhost:8233`.

2. Start a worker against the demo flow, in a second terminal (blocks in
   the foreground; boots the flow's nodes once and keeps them live):

   ```bash
   node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.json
   ```

   On success it prints `worker connected, flowVersion=<hash>,
   taskQueue=node-red-temporal` and keeps running.

3. In a third terminal, start a Workflow Execution that drives the demo
   flow, beginning at its inject node (`n1`):

   ```bash
   node bin/node-red-temporal start --flow demo/flows.json --start-node n1 --input '{"payload":"hello"}'
   ```

   This prints the generated `workflowId` (e.g.
   `node-red-temporal-1700000000000`) and its `runId`, then exits.

4. Check status either via the Temporal CLI:

   ```bash
   temporal workflow describe --workflow-id <workflowId>
   ```

   (`Status: COMPLETED`, with a `Result` containing `flowVersion` and the
   last node reached), or via the Web UI at `http://localhost:8233`, which
   shows the Workflow's Activity list and full event history.

5. Stop the worker with `Ctrl+C` (or `kill <pid>`) once you are done; leave
   the Temporal dev server running if other work still needs it.

## Recovery demo

`demo/flows.recovery-demo.json` is the same shape as `demo/flows.json` with
a `delay` node inserted between the HTTP request and the tagging step,
giving a deliberate window to kill and restart the worker **between**
Activities (not mid-Activity - see Known limitations below) and observe the
Workflow resume from where it left off, without re-running already-completed
Activities. Sequence:

```bash
node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json &
node bin/node-red-temporal start --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json --start-node n1 --input '{"payload":"hello"}'
# while the delay node's window is open, kill the worker, then restart it:
node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json
```

The Workflow completes once the restarted worker's Activity poll picks the
Workflow back up; the Temporal Web UI's event history shows the gap and
resumption.

## Known limitations

- **At-least-once Activity execution.** If the worker process is killed
  while an `executeNode` Activity is mid-flight against a side-effecting
  node (e.g. an `http request` node that already fired its HTTP call),
  Temporal will re-schedule and re-run that same Activity on restart,
  re-firing the side effect. The recovery demo above only demonstrates
  killing the worker **between** Activities, which is safe; mid-Activity
  kills are a known, unresolved limitation of this MVP.
- **Hooks are a process-global singleton.** `RED.hooks` is shared across
  the whole runtime process, not scoped per flow - only one `Capture`
  instance should be installed per worker process.
- **Single-path routing only.** The Workflow (`lib/workflows.js`) follows
  only the first destination on the first port a node actually sent on;
  fan-out to multiple wires or multiple output ports is not implemented.
- **No context durability.** Node and flow context (`context.get`/`.set`)
  remain worker-local, in-memory, and are lost on worker restart.
- **`flowVersion` is pinned with no migration path.** Redeploying a flow
  changes its content hash, which will mismatch and fail any in-flight
  Workflow still referencing the old `flowVersion` - there is no automatic
  migration of in-flight executions to a new flow version.
- **Not tuned for production throughput.** No batching, no worker pooling
  guidance, no benchmarking - this is an MVP proving the execution seam,
  not a production-ready scheduler.

## Architecture

- `lib/capture.js` - `Capture`: installs `preRoute`/`onComplete` (plus a
  scoped, per-invocation `node.error` patch) hooks against a live `RED`
  runtime to observe one node's sends/completion, suppressing local
  delivery (`done(false)`) so Temporal decides the next hop.
- `lib/bootstrap.js` - boots a single `flows.json` headlessly through the
  real `@node-red/runtime` (no HTTP/editor) and computes a canonicalized
  content-hash `flowVersion`.
- `lib/wireGraph.js` - pure transform of flow JSON into a minimal
  `nodeId -> wires` graph, the only per-node routing data passed into a
  Workflow (never full node configs).
- `lib/activities.js` - `createExecuteNode`: the Temporal Activity that
  delivers one message to one live node via `Capture.around()` and returns
  its `{sends, error?}`.
- `lib/workflows.js` - `executeFlow`: the deterministic Temporal Workflow
  that walks the wire graph one `executeNode` Activity call at a time.
- `lib/worker.js` - `createWorker`: wires bootstrap + `Capture` + the
  Activity + the Workflow into a real `@temporalio/worker` `Worker`.
- `bin/node-red-temporal` - CLI: `--flow <path>` runs a worker;
  `start --flow <path> --start-node <id> --input <json>` starts a Workflow
  Execution via `@temporalio/client`.

## Manual MQTT-broker E2E gate

The M6 external-source ingress mechanism (any autonomous, non-Activity-owned
`node.receive()`/`send()` starts exactly one Workflow Execution) has automated,
CI-run unit coverage, but that coverage never touches MQTT's actual wire
protocol. `demo/mqtt-e2e-manual.md` documents a **manual, human-run, not
CI-automated** procedure that wires a real `mqtt in` node
(`demo/flows.mqtt-e2e.json`) to a real external MQTT broker, publishes one
message with the already-installed `mqtt` npm client, and confirms exactly one
Workflow Execution starts and completes. See that document for the full
procedure, pass/fail criteria, and why this is a manual gate rather than an
automated one (issue #11).
